**The Last Tuning**

Walter Hesse had been tuning pianos for fifty-three years, and in all that time he had never gotten used to the silence of a piano that no one played.

The call had come on a Tuesday, from a woman named Delacroix who lived out past the water tower, in one of those old farmhouses that the town had grown around and never quite absorbed. She wanted the piano tuned before her mother arrived for the summer. That was all. He almost declined. His hands had begun to ache in the mornings, and his hearing—the good ear, the one he'd trained against the grain of every string in three counties—had started to blur at the high end, like a radio drifting between stations. He had already told his wife, Ruth, that June would be his last month. He had already begun giving away his tools, one by one, to a young man in the next town over who was learning the trade and didn't yet know that the trade was mostly listening.

But he took the call. He took it because the woman said the piano had belonged to her father, and because she said, in a careful voice, that nobody had played it in eleven years.

He arrived on a Thursday afternoon when the light came in low and yellow through the cottonwoods. The house smelled like dust and closed windows and, faintly, like oranges. Mrs. Delacroix was younger than he'd expected, maybe fifty, with her hair pinned up in a way that suggested she had dressed for the occasion and then forgotten why. She led him down a hallway lined with photographs he did not look at, because looking at other people's photographs on the job was a habit that made the work heavier, and he carried enough already.

The piano sat in a room at the back of the house with southeastern light and a rug worn pale in a半circle in front of the bench. It was an upright, a 1962 Baldwin, walnut, with a bench that opened on a hinge he knew by heart. The fallboard had a scratch across it, long and deliberate, the kind a child makes with a fork or a key, and Walter felt something loosen in his chest. He had a scratch like that on a piano in his own living room, made by a daughter who was now fifty-one and lived in another state.

He opened the lid. The strings were dull with age, spotted here and there with the bloom of corrosion, but they weren't broken. He pressed middle C. The note that came out was so flat it was nearly a different note entirely, and it wavered, and it died fast, the way notes die in a piano that has been left alone—quickly, without echo, without anyone to catch them.

He sat down on the floor beside it and opened his case.

Tuning is not a mysterious art, whatever people like to believe. It is patience, a good ear, and a lever you fit over the tuning pins and turn by millimeters, always millimeters, while you strike the key and listen to the beating between two strings and wait for the beats to slow, and slow, and vanish. Anyone can learn the motions in a year. What takes a lifetime is knowing, before you touch the pin, which way it wants to move, and how much, and when to stop. Every piano has a mind of its own. Some are stubborn, some are loose, some drift back out of tune while you're still working on them, as if they resent the intrusion. The best ones settle under your hands like animals that have decided to trust you.

This one was stubborn. The pins were tight—good pins, they hadn't slipped—and the strings fought him for the first hour. He worked in no hurry. He had stopped hurrying around 1994, the year a doctor told him his back would not forgive him if he didn't, and he had discovered that slowness was not a concession but a method. You heard more when you went slow. You heard the wobble in a unison, the way one string of a three-string unison had gone sour while its sisters held. You heard, if you let yourself, the room.

The room wanted to hear this piano again. He could tell. Some rooms are dead, acoustically—carpeted, curtain-hung, stuffed with furniture that eats sound. This one had a hardwood floor and high windows and nothing in it but the piano, the bench, a lamp, and a plant that was surviving on neglect. The sound rose up out of the strings and came back off the walls a half-beat later, softened, like a reply.

Around five o'clock, Mrs. Delacroix brought him tea he hadn't asked for and stood in the doorway while he drank it.

"My father used to play," she said. "After dinner. Every night. Mostly hymns, and then, when he thought we'd gone to bed, Gershwin."

Walter nodded. He had heard this story, in one form or another, from a thousand people in a thousand rooms. The piano as the furniture of a vanished evening.

"He's been gone eleven years," she said. "My mother's moving in with me in July. She hasn't seen the piano since the funeral." A pause. "I wanted it to be in tune. I don't know if she plays anymore. Her hands, you know."

He said he understood, and he did, and she left him alone again.

He finished at a quarter to seven. The last thing, always, was the stretch of the unisons in the treble, where the strings are shortest and the errors are cruelest, and then a run of scales, soft, just to hear the instrument agree with itself. He played a C major scale and it rose up the keyboard without a single beating interval, clean as water. Then, because the room had been so patient and the woman had told him about the Gershwin, he played a few bars of "Someone to Watch Over Me," quietly, the way you play when you don't want to be caught.

The melody filled the room and went out the open hallway and he did not see whether anyone heard it. He closed the fallboard gently, the way you close a lid on something sleeping, and packed his tools.

Mrs. Delacroix paid him at the door and stood holding the money a moment after he'd taken it, as if she'd forgotten what money was for.

"It sounds like him," she said.

He knew she didn't mean it literally. He knew, also, that she meant it completely. He said good evening, and he walked out into the last of the light, and he did not take another call that June, or any month after. But he thought about that piano for a long time—thought of it sitting in its room of low light, in tune, waiting, which is a thing pianos do better than almost anything else we build. They wait. They hold their hundreds of pounds of tension in the dark for years, and then, if someone sits down and lifts the fallboard, they give back exactly what was asked of them, note for note, as if no time had passed at all.

Or maybe no one ever plays it and he tunes it anyway because that's the work - care without audience.
